description: This course introduces students to global Indigenous artistic traditions, with case studies drawn from cultures including the Lakota (United States), Ainu (Japan), Sámi (Scandinavia), Inuit (Canada), Maori (Aotearoa/New Zealand), and Yanomami (Brazil), among others. Through close analysis of visual and material practices, the course examines how Indigenous artists represent their own communities and how those communities have been represented by others. Students will explore the relationships between art, cultural sovereignty, and knowledge transmission, with particular attention to both tangible and intangible heritage, including artistic practices, oral traditions, and foodways. The course considers the ongoing challenges posed by colonial histories and contemporary museum practices, as well as the strategies Indigenous communities employ to sustain and revitalize cultural traditions. Working closely with objects from the Flaten Art Museum's collection--including a recent acquisition of Inuit prints--students will engage in object-based learning and may participate in collaborative projects with the museum, with emphasis on critical looking, ethical interpretation, and the role of museums in shaping understandings of Indigenous art.
name: Top: Global Indigenous Art
notes: This course includes an academic civic engagement (ACE) component.
